The lighthouse stands on its black rock as the last copper light drains from the western sky. Waves, gone slate-grey and heavy, fold themselves against the base with a slow, patient hush. The white tower, striped faintly red, has lost its colour to the dimming air and become a pale column against the deepening blue. Gulls wheel once more, then vanish into crevices along the cliff.

Then, high in the lantern room, the lamp wakes. A single warm beam swings out across the water, sweeping through the thin mist like a slow, golden hand. It touches the whitecaps, the distant buoy, the far edge of the horizon, and returns again, steady as a heartbeat.

Below, a few windows in the keeper's cottage glow amber. Wind carries the smell of salt and wet stone. Out on the dark water, a fishing boat turns toward the light, trusting it entirely, as sailors always have, as the first stars appear.
